name: Ocean Drive
label: Ocean Drive
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'The Colony Hotel' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'The Colony Hotel' (way/435587753): middle (44 m across); moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OSM W424828682 (Ocean Drive): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Art Deco hotels and neon along South Beach.

text.description:
Ocean Drive is the street most people picture when they think of Miami's Art Deco seafront: a row of pastel-coloured hotel facades, with neon signs that come on as the light fades. The best-known frame is at the Colony Hotel, 736 Ocean Drive. Its lit neon sign and pastel facade are often named as the most photogenic on the street. Standing on the park side of the road, you can fit the sign, the building and a strip of dusk sky into one shot.

The timing matters. Dusk works best, when the neon is lit and there is still some colour left in the sky. Advice online disagrees: some people prefer early morning for emptier streets, others prefer night for the neon. Ocean Drive is also described in recent pages as partly car-free, so check current street closures before you go. Watch for traffic and keep out of the pedestrian flow while you line up the shot.

If you have time for a second picture, try the street-level view of the pastel row stretching away down Ocean Drive. Alternatively, walk into Lummus Park for a cleaner view of the Art Deco facades with fewer people in the frame.
text.geographic_location: Ocean Drive is the seafront street lined with Art Deco hotels, with Lummus Park nearby. The Colony Hotel is at 736 Ocean Drive, and the park-side pavement in front of it is the spot for the classic neon-sign frame.
text.directions_text: Head to Ocean Drive and walk to 736 Ocean Drive, the Colony Hotel. Use the park-side pavement in front of it for the classic neon-sign frame. The Colony Hotel is a separate stop, a short walk north of the subject point, near 8th Street. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to get the sign, the facade and some sky in one frame. If the pavement is too narrow to step back, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x), but keep the sign away from the edges of the picture, where buildings can look stretched.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (park-side sidewalk of Ocean Drive, in front of the hotel at 736 Ocean Drive). The hotel's lit neon sign and pastel Art Deco facade, with a strip of dusk sky above.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the sign on one of the upper third lines, with the facade filling the lower part of the picture and a band of sky above. Keep your phone upright and level so the building doesn't lean. For an alternative, try the street-level view of the pastel row receding down Ocean Drive, or the row of facades from Lummus Park.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the neon sign to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the lit letters keep their colour and don't turn white. As the light drops, night mode can help, but hold the phone steady against your body, or rest your elbows on something solid, while it takes the picture.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Dusk, when the neon is on and there is still some colour in the sky. Early morning is quieter if you prefer empty streets.

text.access_note: This is a public street and pavement, but parts of Ocean Drive may be closed to cars at times, so check current street closures before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The ultra-wide lens can stretch buildings near the edges of the frame.
Lowering the exposure slider helps stop bright neon from turning white.
Night mode needs the phone held steady for a few seconds.

name: Kaseya Center
label: Kaseya Center
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Bayfront Park' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Bayfront Park' (relation/17832054): edge nearest the subject (685 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/25312625: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Kaseya Center' (211 m across).
notes: Arena where the Miami Heat play.

text.description:
Kaseya Center is the big waterfront arena beside Biscayne Bay in downtown Miami, home of the Miami Heat basketball team. It opened on 31 December 1999 as American Airlines Arena and has carried the Kaseya name since April 2023. Arquitectonica was one of the design firms behind it, and the arena holds about 19,500 people. Inside is an unusual scoreboard by the artist Christopher Janney, inspired by sea anemones and able to change colour with the mood of the event.

For a phone photo, the arena works best as part of the downtown waterfront rather than as a close-up. The best-suited spot is Bayfront Park, on the seawall path facing the bay. From the water's edge you can include the open water and the city skyline. The arena sits a short walk to the north, so it will be one building among several. Check the framing on the spot, because it may look small at first. Zooming in a little helps, and you can also try the Maurice A. Ferré Park promenade, which gives a bay-side skyline view with the arena among the waterfront buildings. If you would rather have the building itself, its frontage on Biscayne Boulevard gives a straight-on or slightly angled view of the facade and its large signage, with palm trees along the pavement.

On match or concert days the area gets busy with crowds and traffic, so keep your phone close and look around before you step back to frame a shot.
text.geographic_location: Kaseya Center is in downtown Miami on Biscayne Bay, along the Biscayne Boulevard waterfront. It lies just north of Bayfront Park.
text.directions_text: Head to Bayfront Park in downtown Miami. If you prefer public transport, the arena itself is served by the Metrorail at Government Center station, with a free transfer to the Metromover Omni Loop. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the bay and skyline, then try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the arena closer. You will not need the ultra-wide (0.5x) from here unless you want a lot of sky and water.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Bayfront Park (waterfront seawall path facing the bay). The downtown towers rising behind you with the open bay in front, which can frame the arena among the skyline from the water's edge.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the horizon level, with the water along the bottom third and the skyline above. Place the arena off-centre rather than in the middle. If it looks too small at 1x, zoom in a step or two. For an alternative, try the promenade at Maurice A. Ferré Park, which gives a bay-side view of the skyline with the arena among the waterfront buildings.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the arena to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is washing out. After dark, use night mode and rest your elbows on a railing or wall to keep the shot steady. Keep the phone still for the second or two it needs.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning for soft light, late afternoon for warm tones, or after dark for the lit skyline.

text.access_note: Bayfront Park is free to enter and photography is allowed there, but the arena itself is a ticketed venue for events, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: At 1x from the stand-here point the arena may look small among the skyline, so zooming in can help.
Resting your elbows on a railing or wall helps keep night-mode shots steady.
Match and concert days bring crowds and traffic around Biscayne Boulevard.

name: Vizcaya Museum and Gardens
label: Vizcaya Museum
camera_source: Commons cluster (28 photos). Moved 24 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 20 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/301895039: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Villa Vizcaya' (86 m across).
notes: Italian-style villa and gardens on Biscayne Bay.

text.description: Vizcaya is a winter villa built by the businessman James Deering on the shore of Biscayne Bay. It is now a museum with formal gardens. The house borrows from Italian Renaissance villas, but it was designed in a Mediterranean Revival style with a few Baroque touches. That mix of pale stonework, carved detail and clipped greenery gives you plenty to frame, even on a phone. Most of the villa was built between 1914 and 1922, and Deering stayed in it each winter from 1916 until he died in 1925. The designers adapted European garden ideas to a subtropical climate, using local coral stone trim and planting palms and philodendrons, which were not part of the Tuscan gardens that inspired Vizcaya. The gardens are laid out as a series of 'rooms', including a Secret Garden, a Theatre Garden, a Maze Garden and a Fountain Garden. A raised garden mound acts as the focal point, so there is always another view to find. The estate became a National Historic Landmark in 1994 and is owned by Miami-Dade County. For photographs, think in two scales: the whole facade, and then details such as doorways, statues, balustrades and clipped hedges. The phone icon on the map is very close to the villa, so you will need to step back or go wide to fit the building in. Look for repeating lines in the paths and steps, which lead the eye towards the house. Check the official site before you go for entry arrangements and any rules about photography indoors.
text.geographic_location: Vizcaya stands on the shore of Biscayne Bay in the Coconut Grove neighbourhood of Miami.
text.directions_text: Head for Vizcaya in Coconut Grove, the well-known neighbourhood on Biscayne Bay. The Vizcaya Station of the Miami Metrorail serves the site. Once inside the grounds, go to the phone icon on the map. The villa is only about 20 m to the south-east, so it is a few steps away. The phone icon on the map is about 20 m north-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the facade, because the phone icon on the map is close to the villa. Use the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for carved details and statues.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 20 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the verticals straight so the walls do not lean. Hold the phone level, and place the villa on one of the grid lines rather than dead centre. Then switch to 2x or more for close shots of doorways, stonework and sculpture. A path or flight of steps in the foreground leads the eye towards the house.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the facade to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so pale stone does not turn white. A Live Photo is handy for catching a moment when people walk out of your frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Softer morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters pale stone better than the harsh midday sun. Early in the day may also mean fewer people in your shots.

text.access_note: Vizcaya is a museum and garden open to the public, so tickets and opening times may apply; check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Morning or late-afternoon light is usually softer and more flattering than midday sun in Miami.
Visiting early in the day may mean fewer people in photos.
Photography rules inside the villa may differ from those in the gardens.
Pale stone can be overexposed by a phone in bright sun.

name: Bayside Marketplace
label: Bayside Marketplace
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Miamarina at Bayside' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Residences at Bayside - by Elite City Stays' (pois); moved 20 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/17832055: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Bayside Marketplace' (592 m across).
notes: Waterfront shopping area with marina views.

text.description:
Bayside Marketplace is an open-air shopping and entertainment complex on the edge of Biscayne Bay, right beside PortMiami. It is made up of two buildings, the North Pavilion and the South Pavilion, and it opened on 8 April 1987. The architect, Benjamin C. Thompson, gave it the look of old market sheds, and it opens out onto a marina called the Miamarina. It was built on a site of about 16 acres.

For photographs, the marina side is the one to head for. Rows of yachts sit in the foreground, and across the water the downtown skyline stands behind them. Around sunset the buildings are reflected in the bay, which gives you a simple, layered picture: boats, water, skyline. Many boat tours leave from this area, so a vessel pulling away from the docks can add something to the frame without any effort from you.

Keep the docks low in the picture, with the skyline filling the upper half. If you want a higher view, there is a bridge at Bayside that looks over the port and the bay. Bayfront Park is another recommended viewpoint, giving you palm trees and grass in front of the same skyline, with a sunrise option over the water.

Expect it to be busy on weekend evenings. Arrive a little before sunset, find a gap along the waterfront, and give yourself time to try a few framings before the light fades.
text.geographic_location: Bayside Marketplace is in Greater Downtown Miami, on the banks of Biscayne Bay next to PortMiami. The City of Miami marina (the Miamarina) lies along one side of it.
text.directions_text: Get to Bayside Marketplace on the bay, next to PortMiami, from Downtown Miami. From there, walk to the marina and the docks on the bay side of the complex. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x), which fits the yachts and the skyline in one frame. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the docks and boats in the foreground. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pull the skyline closer, or to pick out a single boat.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (waterfront marina, Biscayne Bay side of the complex). Yacht-lined docks in the foreground with the downtown skyline reflected across the bay, especially at sunset. The marina and its bay-side docks are a short walk away.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and put the horizon on the lower or upper third line. Keep the docks and boats in the foreground and the skyline behind them. If you want a higher viewpoint, the bridge at Bayside looks over the port and the bay, and Bayfront Park is another recommended viewpoint, with palm trees and a sunrise option over the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the skyline to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour. After sunset, use night mode and brace your phone against a rail or your own arm to keep it steady. Try a Live Photo when a boat is leaving the dock, so you can pick the best moment afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset, when the skyline is reflected across the bay. Weekend evenings are busy, so arrive early.

text.access_note: Bayside is an open-air shopping and entertainment complex whose shops and restaurants have their own rules, so check the official site before you go.

name: Bayfront Park
label: Bayfront Park
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Baywalk' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Baywalk nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/17832054: large area 'Bayfront Park' (688 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Downtown waterfront park with skyline views.

text.description: Bayfront Park is a 32-acre public park on the edge of Downtown Miami, running along Biscayne Bay. It opened in March 1925, and from 1980 the artist and landscape architect Isamu Noguchi reworked it, so it has sculpture, open lawns and a long waterfront edge. For photographs, that gives you three things to choose from: the wide bay, the city towers and a few strong landmarks. The Torch of Friendship, built in 1960, stands at the north-west corner. The Challenger Memorial, a 100-foot spiralling steel sculpture, is at the south-west corner. The Pepper Fountain on the eastern side was renovated and reopened in February 2025, and can now throw water up to about 150 feet (46 m). The best skyline-and-water pictures come from the bayfront path called Baywalk, where the view across the water is open and nothing gets in the way. The fountain is a good foreground subject with the towers behind it, and the Torch works well as a main subject with the park around it. The park is big, so decide on your subject first and walk to it rather than trying to get everything from one spot. Leave a little time for the walk between viewpoints.
text.geographic_location: Bayfront Park is in the Central Business District of Downtown Miami, on the shore of Biscayne Bay. It sits between Biscayne Boulevard and the water, with Bayside Marketplace to its north.
text.directions_text: Head for the Biscayne Boulevard side of Downtown Miami and the park. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the open bay and sky, and switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look at the skyline. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the fountain jets or the Torch of Friendship from a distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Baywalk (bayfront seawall path, toward the Bayside Marketplace end). An open view across Biscayne Bay with the downtown towers rising behind the photographer and no obstructions in the frame. From here you have an open view across Biscayne Bay with nothing in the frame, and the downtown towers rise behind you, so turn around to take in the city.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and set the horizon on a line so the water and skyline sit straight. Keep some water in the lower part of the frame to give the picture depth. For something different, walk into the park and frame the fountain jets in the foreground with the towers behind, or take the Torch of Friendship as the main subject with the park and bay around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the sky or the towers to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour. If you shoot the fountain in the evening, use night mode and hold the phone steady against the railing or your body.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning gives soft golden light, and late afternoon gives warm amber tones on the towers.

text.access_note: Baywalk and the park are open public space, but events can limit access, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Baywalk is a free public path with an open view of Biscayne Bay and no obstructions in the frame.
From Baywalk the downtown towers rise behind a photographer facing the bay.
Early morning gives soft golden light and late afternoon gives warm amber tones on the towers.
The fountain show runs mainly in the evening, and events can limit access to the fountain rim.
The stand-here point on Baywalk is roughly 10-12 minutes on foot south of the middle of the park (from the supplied distance of 915 m).
Night mode will help with evening shots of the fountain.

name: Wynwood Walls
label: Wynwood Walls
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'NW 2nd Avenue' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Northwest 2nd Avenue' (way/49239038): point nearest the subject (932 m long).
pin_note: Position from OSM W311836305 (Wynwood Walls): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.

text.description:
Wynwood Walls is a gated complex of large murals in Miami's Wynwood district, and its outer walls and the streets around it are full of colour. This spot is about the street view, which is the free way to photograph it, because the outside of the complex can be shot from the pavement without going through the gates. That gives you a lively background and plenty of choice.

The main complex is ticketed, with entry through the Welcome Center on NW 26th Street, so check the official site before you go if you want to go inside. Murals here are repainted often, so the wall you saw in a picture online may have changed. Treat that as part of the fun and photograph whatever is up on the day.

For a phone, the challenge is fitting a big wall into the frame without stepping into traffic. The ultra-wide lens (0.5x) helps, so you can stay on the pavement. Keep your phone level, switch on the gridlines to keep the wall's edges straight, and take one wide shot plus a closer one of a single mural. Please keep walkways clear and don't stand on painted pavement.
text.geographic_location: Wynwood Walls is in the Wynwood district of Miami, on NW 2nd Avenue (listed at 2516 NW 2nd Ave), with the Welcome Center on NW 26th Street.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Wynwood area of Miami and check local transport options for the best way to reach NW 2nd Avenue. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit a whole wall in from the pavement, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a cleaner, less stretched view of one mural. If your phone has a telephoto lens (2x-5x), use it to pick out details from across the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on NW 2nd Avenue (sidewalk and street in front of the gated Wynwood Walls complex). The outer walls of the Wynwood Walls complex and its large murals, framed from the street with the mural-covered blocks running off to either side.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line a wall's edge up with a vertical line so the building doesn't lean. Take one wide frame showing the walls running along the street, then a tighter one of a single mural. A wide lens may not fit the whole wall from the pavement, so use 0.5x rather than stepping into the road.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the wall to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the paint colours stay rich and the sky doesn't wash out. Hold the phone level for the wide shots.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning, before about 11 AM, when it is quieter and the shadows are softer. Avoid the harsh glare around noon to 3 PM.

text.access_note: The streets outside are public and free to photograph from the pavement, but the main Wynwood Walls complex is ticketed and its hours and rules change, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Facing west from the stand-here point on NW 2nd Avenue in the morning, the sun should be behind you or to your side and light the wall.
A tap-to-focus and exposure slider adjustment helps keep bright mural colours rich on most phones.
The ultra-wide lens (0.5x) lets you fit more of a wall in than the default lens (1x) from the same spot.

name: Casa Casuarina
label: Versace Mansion
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Ocean Drive' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Ocean Drive nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/380875533: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'The Villa Casa Casuarina' (45 m across).
notes: Former home of Gianni Versace on Ocean Drive.

text.description:
Casa Casuarina, also known as the Versace Mansion, is a Mediterranean Revival house at 1116 Ocean Drive in South Beach. It was finished in 1930 for Alden Freeman, a philanthropist and Standard Oil heir, who said he modelled it on the Alcázar de Colón. The designer Gianni Versace lived here from 1992 until 1997. Since 2015 it has run as a boutique hotel, The Villa Casa Casuarina, with ten suites.

It photographs well because the front is so clear and formal. Wrought-iron gates sit above pale coquina steps, and the carved stonework and wall medallions give you plenty of texture. The front steps are widely described as the most photographed part of the house, and the straight-on view from the street is the one most people picture first. The house is a private hotel, so everything here is shot from the public sidewalk.

Stand on the Ocean Drive sidewalk facing the gates and keep your phone level so the walls stay straight. Fit the whole facade in, including the steps at the bottom, then take a closer shot of a doorway, medallion or gate detail. If the pavement is busy, wait a moment for a gap in the passers-by. For a different view, the corner of 11th Street gives a side-on angle along the southern edge of the property. Keep your photos to what you can see from the street.
text.geographic_location: Casa Casuarina is in the South Beach neighbourhood of Miami Beach, Florida, on Ocean Drive close to the corner with 11th Street. It lies within the Miami Beach Architectural District.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or similar stop is listed for this spot, so start from the South Beach area of Miami Beach and head for 1116 Ocean Drive, by taxi or hired scooter if you are coming from further away. Once on Ocean Drive, look for the mansion's wrought-iron gates and pale stone steps. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the full facade. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if the sidewalk is so narrow that you cannot fit the gates and steps in. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the carved stonework, medallions and gate details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Ocean Drive (sidewalk directly in front of the mansion's wrought-iron gates and coquina steps). The full Mediterranean Revival facade with its front steps and gate, framed straight on from the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the gate up with the middle of the frame so the facade looks even on both sides. Keep the steps in the bottom of the picture to give the shot some depth. For an alternative, walk to the 11th Street corner for a side-on view along the southern edge of the property.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the bright sky or white walls look washed out. Hold the phone level to avoid leaning walls.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning light is suggested for showing off the architectural detail.

text.access_note: The house is a private hotel and members' property whose courtyard, pool and interiors are for guests and diners only, so photograph from the public sidewalk and check the official site before you go.

name: Phillip and Patricia Frost Museum of Science
label: Frost Science
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'The Vista' (4 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Northeast 34th Street & Buena Vista Boulevard' (pois).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/319426548: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Patricia and Phillip Frost Museum of Science' (213 m across).

text.description:
The Phillip and Patricia Frost Museum of Science is a science museum, planetarium and aquarium on the downtown waterfront, next to the Pérez Art Museum Miami. It opened in Museum Park on 8 May 2017, after the old Coconut Grove museum closed in 2015. The complex has four interconnected buildings, and its centrepiece is a three-storey, cone-shaped aquarium holding about 500,000 US gallons.

For a phone photo, the best viewpoint is The Vista, the open-air rooftop terrace at the top of the Aquarium. From the rooftop you can see the Downtown Miami skyline and Biscayne Bay behind the surface of the Gulf Stream tank, with the Port of Miami close by. Several visitor guides name this rooftop as the best skyline view at the museum, and one suggests arriving about an hour before sunset for clear views and cruise ships at PortMiami.

Inside, the 31-foot circular Oculus window at the bottom of the tank is another good shot. Sharks, rays and mahi-mahi swim overhead, and the cone of the tank frames the picture. The museum sits in Maurice A. Ferré Park.

The Vista and the Oculus are both inside the museum, so you need a ticket. Flash is not allowed in the aquarium areas, and planetarium shows generally cannot be photographed while they run.
text.geographic_location: The museum is in Museum Park (Maurice A. Ferré Park) on the Biscayne Bay waterfront in downtown Miami, next to the Pérez Art Museum Miami.
text.directions_text: No Metrorail, Metromover or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from downtown Miami and head to the Biscayne Bay waterfront in Museum Park, next to the Pérez Art Museum Miami. Once there, enter the museum and go up to the top open-air level of the Aquarium. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the skyline, the bay and the tank surface together. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the terrace and the sky. Use the telephoto/zoom (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out cruise ships at PortMiami or the towers on the skyline.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on The Vista (top open-air level of the Aquarium (rooftop terrace)). Downtown Miami skyline and Biscayne Bay in the background, with the Gulf Stream tank surface and the Port of Miami nearby. Find a spot at the edge where you can see all of these.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the skyline along the upper third, with the tank surface or the water in the lower part to give depth. Zoom in on the port for a tighter shot of the ships. For a second picture, use the Oculus indoors and shoot up through the window so the swimming sharks and rays are framed by the cone of the tank.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the skyline to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour near sunset. Keep flash off, as it is restricted in the aquarium areas. At the Oculus, tap on a fish to focus and take a few Live Photos or quick bursts, because the animals keep moving.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: About an hour before sunset, when the rooftop views are reported to be clear and cruise ships may be at the port. Check the official site for rooftop access on the day.

text.access_note: The Vista and the Oculus are inside the ticketed museum and are separate from the map's stand-here point, so check the official site before you go for tickets and rooftop access.

text.description:
Pérez Art Museum Miami, usually called PAMM, is a contemporary art museum on Biscayne Bay in Downtown Miami. Its building, by the Swiss architects Herzog & de Meuron, opened in December 2013. The design takes its cue from Stiltsville, the wooden houses on stilts off Key Biscayne, so the galleries sit above a deep, shaded veranda with wide overhanging canopies. Hanging vertical gardens by the French botanist Patrick Blanc, made up of around 80 kinds of plants, drape down from the canopy. A grand staircase nearly 180 feet wide links the building to the waterfront.

The museum photographs well because it is long, low and strongly horizontal, and it sits above green lawns and palms. The best view of the whole building is from the sloped lawn of Maurice A. Ferré Park, which is about 20 acres and stretches out in front of it. From there you can take in the full facade with the planting in the foreground. If you want a second angle, the shaded ground-floor veranda is a good place for pictures with the hanging plant columns overhead and the bay beyond. The sculpture garden is another option, with outdoor sculptures among palms and the museum behind them.

Take a wide shot first, then move closer for details such as the plant columns, the staircase and the shadows under the canopy. Rules on photography inside the galleries can vary by exhibition, so ask staff before taking pictures indoors.
text.geographic_location: In Downtown Miami, on the Biscayne Bay waterfront inside Maurice A. Ferré Park, on Biscayne Boulevard.
text.directions_text: The museum is in Downtown Miami at 1103 Biscayne Boulevard, and the Museum Park Metromover station serves it directly. Once you are in the park, walk onto the sloped lawn in front of the museum and turn to face the building. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close to the building and want the whole long facade in one frame. Step back and use the default lens (1x) for a more natural, less stretched look. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the hanging plant columns and the staircase.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Maurice A. Ferré Park (sloped lawn in front of the museum, facing the building). The full long facade of the museum rising over the green lawns and palms in front of it. For the full-facade shot, walk south-west to the sloped lawn of Maurice A.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the long horizontal edge of the building up with one of them, so the facade looks level. Leave some lawn and palms at the bottom of the frame to give the shot depth. For a different view, try the shaded veranda, with the plant columns overhead and the bay beyond, or the sculpture garden, with the museum and bay behind the sculptures.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the bright sky is washing out the facade. Hold the phone steady and take a few frames so you can pick the sharpest.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer harsh shadows under the canopy. Midday sun is brighter and more contrasty.

text.access_note: The park is open to the public and reachable on foot, but museum entry and some museum grounds may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning or late afternoon light is usually softer and gives fewer harsh shadows than midday.
Photography rules inside the galleries can vary by exhibition, so ask staff before taking pictures indoors.
The bayfront grounds and veranda may be free to enter while the galleries are paid; this needs checking against the museum's current entry rules.

text.description: South Pointe Park is a 17-acre park at the very southern tip of South Beach, where Miami Beach meets the channel into the Port of Miami. It opened on 25 October 1985 and was redesigned by Hargreaves Associates, with the work finishing around March 2009. The wide limestone-edged walkways date from that rebuild. It photographs well because so much sits close together: beach, lawns, the channel with ships passing, Fisher Island, the downtown Miami skyline and the open Atlantic. For a first photo, walk out on South Pointe Pier and turn back toward the park. From there you can frame the shoreline and beach with the lifeguard tower and the South Beach hotels behind. The pier is recommended for sunrise, but the shot back toward the park may not show the sun. The open sea and passing ships are in the opposite direction, so turn around if you want to include one. If you would rather shoot the skyline, the channel-side lawns and seawall look across the water to downtown and Fisher Island. A grassy rise inside the park is a quieter alternative to the pier, with greenery in the foreground and the bay or skyline behind. Pick one main view, then walk a few minutes to a second. Wipe your lens before you start, as sea air leaves a fine film that softens phone photos. Weekends can be busy, so early morning gives you the clearest views.
text.geographic_location: South Pointe Park is at the southern end of South Beach in Miami Beach, beside Government Cut and the entrance to the Port of Miami. It looks across the water to Fisher Island and downtown Miami.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot, so use a map app to get from South Beach to the southern tip of Miami Beach. Follow the main walkways toward the water and the pier. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the shoreline, beach and hotels. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the pier rails and the sky. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out a ship on the horizon when you turn to face the open sea.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on South Pointe Pier (shot back toward the park from the pier, facing the beach side). The park's shoreline and beach at sunrise, with the lifeguard tower and South Beach hotels behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the waterline on a lower third line so the beach, buildings and sky each get space. Use the pier rail or edge as a leading line for depth. For the skyline instead, walk to the channel-side lawns and seawall, or try the grassy rise in the park for a quieter view.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the main subject, such as the beach or the lifeguard tower, to focus. If the sky looks too bright, slide the exposure down a little so the colours do not wash out. Try a Live Photo, so you can choose the best frame if people walk through.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: The pier is recommended for sunrise, though the view back toward the park may not show the sun itself. The open sea and ships are in the opposite direction. For the skyline, the park lawns in the evening are a good choice.

text.access_note: South Pointe Park is a public park, but access to the pier and its closing times can change, so check the official site before you go.

text.description: Lincoln Road Mall is a long, car-free stretch of Miami Beach lined with shops, restaurants and galleries. It runs east to west between 16th Street and 17th Street. It began as a strip cleared through the mangroves in 1912, and in the 1950s architect Morris Lapidus redesigned it in his playful Miami Modern ("MiMo") style. It opened as a pedestrian mall in November 1960, one of the first in the country, and it is now on the National Register of Historic Places. For a phone photo, its strength is the straight line of the walkway. Palm trees and shopfronts recede into the distance, and people strolling through the scene give it life. The best classic view is from the Washington Avenue end, looking west down the mall. Because there is no traffic, you can stand in the walkway and take your time, though it is a busy place, so keep to the side. If you want a change from the long view, the Art Deco front of the restored Colony Theatre makes a good second picture. Soundscape Park is a quieter alternative, with public sculptures in the foreground and the storefronts behind them. Look for people, palms and shop signs to give the long view depth, and take a few frames as passers-by move through.
text.geographic_location: Lincoln Road Mall is in South Beach, Miami Beach, running between 16th Street and 17th Street. It stretches from Washington Avenue in the east to Alton Road in the west.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so go by taxi or hired scooter to the Washington Avenue end of Lincoln Road Mall in South Beach. From there, walk onto the car-free mall and look west. The rest of the mall lies ahead of you, and you can walk on to the Colony Theatre or Soundscape Park if you want other views. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the long view down the mall. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the palms and shopfronts at the sides. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out a detail, such as the Colony Theatre front or a row of palms.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Lincoln Road and Washington Avenue (at the Washington Avenue end, looking west down the mall). A long, straight view down the pedestrian promenade, with palm trees and the street's shops and storefronts receding toward the west. A historical marker stands at this corner, so it is easy to recognise.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and put the middle of the walkway on the centre line so the shopfronts lead the eye down the street. Keep your phone level so the buildings do not lean. Wait for a few people to walk through the middle distance to give a sense of scale. For a different view, the Colony Theatre's Art Deco front works well with the mall's activity and palms around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the middle of the street to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright so the shopfronts stay detailed. Use night mode after dark, and hold the phone steady against your body or a solid surface.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is usually calmer and gives cleaner frames with fewer people. Late afternoon and evening bring warmer light and lit-up shops, but you will be facing the sun, so expect some glare and check your exposure.

text.access_note: Lincoln Road Mall is an open, car-free public street, so you can photograph it freely for personal use. Commercial shoots may need a permit, so check the official Miami Beach site before you go.

text.description:
Española Way is a short, car-free lane in South Beach, lined with pink and peach Mediterranean Revival buildings, balconies and restaurant tables. It is one of the easiest places on the map to get a good phone photo, because the buildings do the framing for you. Strings of lights hang across the lane, and the colours look soft and warm in evening light.

South Beach is the part of Miami Beach south of Dade Boulevard. It was the first section of the island to be developed, starting in the 1910s, and it is best known for its 1930s Art Deco, Streamline Moderne and Nautical Moderne buildings. Española Way gives you a gentler, more Mediterranean look, which makes it a good contrast to the seafront.

The classic picture is taken from the middle of the pedestrian block, looking west down the lane. The walkway leads the eye away from you, the lights run overhead and the pastel facades sit on both sides. If you also want a wider scene-setter, walk to the entrance of the lane, where a welcome sign is reported and the lane opens up ahead with restaurants and balconies on either side.

The street is pedestrian-only, so you don't have to dodge traffic. It does get busy with people dining outside, especially after dark, so be patient and wait for a gap. Sunset or just after, when the string lights come on, is the best time.
text.geographic_location: Española Way is in South Beach, the southern part of Miami Beach, on the Atlantic side of Miami. The lane's entrance is likely at its Washington Avenue end.
text.directions_text: Travel to South Beach by whatever means suits you and finish on foot. Once you are on the lane, walk to the middle of the pedestrian block, which is the usual spot for the view looking west. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the classic view down the lane. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the whole lit canopy and both rows of buildings, and keep people away from the edges of the frame, where they can look stretched. Use telephoto (2x or more) to pack the string lights closer together.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Española Way (middle of the pedestrian block, looking west down the lane). The pedestrian lane running away from the camera, with string lights overhead and pink and peach Mediterranean Revival buildings on both sides. For a second, wider view, go to the entrance of the lane, where a welcome sign is reported and the lane opens up ahead lined with restaurants and balconies.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the middle of the lane on the centre line, so the buildings look balanced on each side. Hold the phone at chest height and keep it level so the facades stay straight. Wait for a gap in the people, or let a few walkers stay in the frame to give a sense of scale. Take the entrance and welcome-sign view as a separate shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the lane to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the string lights stay bright and don't wash out. As it gets dark, switch on night mode and brace your elbows against your body or lean on something solid so the shot stays sharp. A Live Photo can catch people drifting through the scene.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset or after dark, when the string lights come on.

text.access_note: This is a pedestrian-only public street, but check the official site before you go for any events or closures.
claims_not_in_sources: The lane's entrance is likely at its Washington Avenue end, and a welcome sign is reported there.
The middle of the pedestrian block is the usual spot for the view looking west, but the exact position is a best reading.
Outdoor dining crowds can block the view, especially at night.
Ultra-wide lenses can stretch people at the edges of the frame.

text.description:
The Freedom Tower is a Spanish Revival building at 600 Biscayne Boulevard, on Miami Dade College's Wolfson Campus. It was built in 1925 as the home of the newspaper The Miami News, and its design borrows from the Giralda in Seville. The cupola sits on a tower 255 feet (78 m) tall. In the 1960s the US government used the building to process and help refugees arriving from Cuba. That role earned it National Historic Landmark status in 2008. Today it is a museum and cultural centre linked to the college, and it reopened in September 2025 after a long restoration.

It photographs well because the shape is so clear: a slim, decorated tower rising above a wide road. The long run of the road leads the eye straight to it, which makes this the natural postcard angle. Keep the whole tower in the frame, with a little sky above the cupola, and use the gridlines to keep the sides of the building upright. Cars and passers-by will cross your shot, so wait for a gap or let a bit of movement add life to the picture. If you want the tower lit up, come back after dark.
text.geographic_location: In downtown Miami, on the Wolfson Campus of Miami Dade College, facing Biscayne Boulevard.
text.directions_text: The Metromover's Freedom Tower station on the Omni Loop serves the building, and the Metrorail's Government Center and Historic Overtown/Lyric Theatre stations are also listed as serving it. If you are coming from elsewhere in Miami, a taxi to 600 Biscayne Boulevard is the simplest option. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the front of the tower with the road leading to it. If the top is cut off, try the ultra-wide (0.5x), but keep the phone level so the tower does not lean. Use the telephoto (2x or more) for a tighter shot of the cupola.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Biscayne Boulevard (east side of the tower, on the boulevard in front of the east façade (the tower faces east onto the road)). The tower's front façade framed by the wide boulevard, with the road leading the eye straight to the building.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the tower on one of the vertical lines so the road runs towards it. Leave a little sky above the cupola. Stay on the pavement and keep clear of traffic. A telephoto shot of the cupola and its decoration makes a good second picture.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the tower to set focus. Then slide the exposure down a touch so the sky stays blue and the tower keeps its detail. After dark, use night mode and hold the phone against a post or your chest to keep it steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Mid-morning or early evening for the best light. Night is worth a visit to see the tower lit up.

text.access_note: You can photograph the outside from the public street, but the tower is a museum, so check the official site before you go for current access to the inside.
claims_not_in_sources: Cars and pedestrians on Biscayne Boulevard may cross the view, so take care near the road.
A night-mode shot is easier if the phone is braced against a fixed object.
Mid-morning and early evening light suit the east-facing front of the tower.

text.description:
The Holocaust Memorial of Miami Beach is a solemn open-air memorial, and its most striking feature is a tall bronze arm and hand reaching up out of a pool. The arm is covered in climbing figures, and the water reflects it. That mix of strong shape, still water and surrounding greenery makes it work well on a phone, even for a quick shot.

The first view of the hand is often from the street. The memorial is on Meridian Avenue, at the corner with Dade Boulevard, near the Convention Center. From there you shoot back toward the hand, with the pool and the greenery around it. It is a free, open-air spot and makes a good street-level picture before you go in.

For a calmer composition with fewer people in it, you can also photograph the memorial from a distance with the Miami Beach Botanical Garden's greenery behind it. If you go inside, the close view of the outstretched arm and its figures, with the pool reflecting it, is the picture most visitors come for.

This is a place of remembrance, so take your photos quietly and keep other visitors out of the frame where you can. Opening hours can vary, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: In Miami Beach, on Meridian Avenue at its corner with Dade Boulevard, close to the Convention Center.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stops are listed for this spot. Head for the Convention Center area of Miami Beach, on foot or by taxi, and ask for Meridian Avenue at Dade Boulevard. Check the official site before you go for current access and opening times. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to frame the hand with the pool and greenery. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the pool and surroundings, and keep the hand away from the edges of the frame so it does not stretch. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the figures on the arm.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Meridian Avenue and Dade Boulevard (the corner by the memorial's street frontage, shooting back toward the hand). The memorial's tall hand seen from the street, set against the pool and the surrounding greenery.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the hand on one of the vertical lines, with the pool and greenery filling the rest of the frame. Hold the phone level so the arm looks upright. For a calmer, less crowded alternative, try the view from a distance with the Miami Beach Botanical Garden's greenery behind the memorial.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the hand to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky does not wash out the dark bronze. Take a few shots in case people walk through the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Visit when the memorial is open and the light is soft, in the morning or later in the day, and check the official site for current hours.

text.access_note: The street view is from open public ground, but photography at this solemn site should be respectful, and you should check the official site before you go for visiting hours and access.

name: Máximo Gómez Park
label: Domino Park
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Máximo Gómez Park' (4 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/318011819: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Máximo Gómez Park' (32 m across).
notes: Little Havana park where locals play dominoes.

text.description:
Máximo Gómez Park is a small green space on Calle Ocho (8th Street) in Little Havana, named after a hero of Cuba's War of Independence. Locals know it as "Domino Park". Since the early 1970s it has been a place where Cuban immigrants meet to drink coffee, smoke cigars and play dominoes, and it has also become a place visitors come to see that daily routine. It hosts food tours, art festivals and other cultural events too.

It photographs well because everything sits close together: the covered concrete domino tables, the players leaning over their games, the trees around the edge and the murals behind. The scene is about people and atmosphere rather than one grand view, so a wide frame that shows the whole setting works best.

The players are not performing, and the tables are reserved for club members, so watch and shoot from the public edge, outside the fenced game area. Some players do not want to be photographed. Ask first before any close portrait, and accept a no with a smile. If you want a second picture, the park's entrance on Calle Ocho is a good alternative, with the painted-domino pavers in the foreground and Little Havana storefronts behind.
text.geographic_location: In Little Havana, Miami, on Calle Ocho (SW 8th Street), among the street's storefronts. The exact frontage may differ slightly, so check on the day.
text.directions_text: No Metrorail or tram stop is listed for this spot, so navigate to Calle Ocho in Little Havana on the map. Once you are on the street, follow the map to the phone icon on the map; the park is a small green space on Calle Ocho. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the main wide shot. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you need to fit in the tables, trees and murals from a tight spot. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for details from further away.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here the photo shows the covered concrete domino tables and the players in one wide frame, with the surrounding trees and murals around them.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the covered tables in the middle third, with trees and murals filling the sides. Keep people small in the frame for a scene shot. For a closer image, zoom in rather than walking up to the tables. For a different view, shoot the entrance from Calle Ocho, with the painted-domino pavers leading the eye towards the tables.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a player or table to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the bright street washes out the shaded area. Only use portrait mode once you have asked someone and they have agreed.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late morning, when street activity is strongest. A weekday morning is likely to feel quieter and less touristy.

text.access_note: Visitors watch and photograph from outside the tables, which are reserved for club members. Check hours and access locally before you go.
